## The brief:

This coursework is made up of four parts. 1. A Jupyter notebook of basic
Python tasks, 2. A Jupyter notebook of basic R tasks, 3. A coding
challenge based around a pumpkins dataset to be completed in **either**
R or Python 4. A coding challenge based around gene expression analysis
datasets, to be completed in **either** R or Python

Exactly **one** of 3 and 4 must be completed in each language. If you
chose to use R to complete the gene expression analysis challenge, you
must use Python to complete the Pumpkins challenge. If you use Python to
complete the gene expression analysis challenge, you must use R to
complete the Pumpkins challenge.

You will create a fork of the LIFE4138_2526 github repository in your
own github account (we will help you to do this). You will delete all
files and directories from the forked repository other than the
Coursework directory. You will then complete the coursework, saving your
answers to the R and Python jupyter notebooks and for each of the two
coding challenges (gene expression and pumpkins analysis) you will
upload:

\- One R or Python script file\
- One requirements script (detailing packages/modules that your script
requires)\
- One report (in a document format of your choosing. This could be, for
example, a markdown or word document), detailing the findings/plots
generated by your script\
- Possibly a filtered dataset output by your code, depending on the
challenge\
- The completed Jupyter notebooks.

Make sure you organise your github repository with care, naming your
documents correctly and structuring directories sensibly.

## The submission:

Your work must be submitted through Moodle, in the form of a single
zipped folder.

This folder should be a zipped download of your completed github
repository. It should contain **every** element of all parts of the
coursework.

## The weightings:

-   This assesment represents 75% of your module mark, and is split
    equally between the two languages.
-   The contents of your R git repo represents 37.5% of the total module
    mark.
-   The contents of your Python git repo also represents 37.5% of the
    total module mark.

## To access your coursework:

### The notebooks:

-   Open a terminal window
-   Activate your lectures conda environment `conda activate lectures`
-   Install R into your lectures conda environment (if it isn't already
    there) `conda install r r-tidyverse r-irkernel ipykernel`
-   If you don't have the LIFE4138 repo, download it using

`git clone https://github.com/BioinformaticsMSc/LIFE4138_2526`

-   Run jupyter lab from your terminal `jupyter lab`

-   Find the coursework inside the LIFE4138_2526 folder in jupyter lab

-   Complete the answers in the empty cells

-   **Make sure you press save!!!**

-   If you are struggling to install R into your conda environment,
    Laura has provided a `.yml` file to construct a new coursework conda
    environment (like you did with the lectures env in week 1!).

### The coding challenges:

-   There are two scripting challenges, you must complete BOTH, one
    using R and one using Python. You can choose which challenge you do
    in which language.
-   The coursework is in the class repo
-   Each challenge has it's own subdirectory within the coursework
    folder.
-   You will each use a different dataset to complete these challenges
    with...
-   The individual datasets are in the challenge subdirectories,
    alongside instructions and a
    `student_dataset_allocation_numbers.txt` file.
-   Use the dataset allocations file to work out which datasets you
    should use to complete the challenges.

## Tips:

-   Read the instructions carefully and check that you have uploaded
    everything required.
-   Comment your code clearly and carefully
-   Ensure you allow for missing or malformed data in your datasets
-   Your code needs to run on an unseen dataset (with the same column
    names), as well as the one you've been allocated - bear that in mind
    when creating your code.
-   Part of each task involves generating a report: this should be well
    structured, including headings, paragraphs, and numbered legends for
    tables and figures to ensure readability and clarity of results.

## The pumpkins coding challenge:

### The data:

For this challenge, you will each be given a unique version of a dataset
named `pumpkins.csv`. This dataset contains modified information about
the competitive growing of giant pumpkins from the official webside of
the Global Pumpkin Commonwealth (yes, really).

The rows of this dataset consist of entries to pumpkin competitions
across the world from 2013 to 2021. The columns key is below, but
remember that much like "real" Biological data, *not all columns are
relevant to the task*!

-   `id` - the year and type of the competition
-   `place` - the place and ranking in the competition
-   `weight_lbs` - the weight of the pumpkin in pounds
-   `grower_name` - name of the grower
-   `city` - city pumpkin was grown in
-   `state_prov` - state or province of grower
-   `country` - country of grower
-   `gpc_site` - great pumpkin commonwealth site
-   `seed_mother` - seed mother
-   `pollinator_father` - father
-   `ott` - over the top inches - for estimating weight
-   `est_weight` - estimated weight in lbs
-   `pct_chart` - percentage on chart
-   `variety` - pumpkin variety

### Your task:

For this part of your coursework, you will write an R or Python script
that will read in the dataset provided for you, modify, summarise, and
extract information from this dataset, generate some plots, and then
save both the plots and the modified dataset to your local machine. You
must then upload your script along with any accompanying files
(described below) to your forked github repository.

You may use any R packages or Python modules that you wish to complete
this challenge. You will submit a `requirements.txt` file which lists
the modules or packages that your script requires to run. You must load
packages/import modules in your script, but you can assume that they are
already installed and do not need to include the code to install them in
your coursework.

Part of the mark for this coursework will come from the outcome of
running your script on a dataset which is similar, but subtly different
from the one you have been given. This test dataset will have the same
column names, but the information contained within the columns will
differ. You will therefore need to ensure that your script can be run
from start to finish without generating errors.

Make sure to comment all of your code thoroughly so that it is clear
what each line is setting out to achieve.

#### Your script must achieve the following:

1.  Read in the pumpkins.csv data.
2.  Identify the heaviest pumpkin grown in any of the competitions –
    what variety was it? Where was it from and when was it grown?
3.  Write a function to change the weight in pounds (lbs) to kilograms
    (kg) and use this function to create a new column in your data set
    called weight_kg.
4.  Create another new column in your data set called weight_class. This
    column should be a factor with three levels: light, medium and heavy
    and should be based on the weight of the pumpkins. You can choose
    the thresholds for these three groups yourself.
5.  Plot the relationship between the estimated weight and actual weight
    of the pumpkins. This can be in either lbs or kg but remember to
    ensure that both axes are in the same units. Colour the points in
    your plot based on the weight_class column that you created in
    question 4. Ensure the plot has appropriate axis labels and is clear
    and well presented. Save this plot to your computer.
6.  Filter the data to include only pumpkins from three countries of
    your choosing and save this filtered data set to your computer in
    csv format.
7.  Summarise your filtered dataset from question 6: a. Identify the
    mean weight of pumpkins for each of your three countries. Which
    country had the highest mean pumpkin weight? b. Identify the mean
    weight for each variety of pumpkin for each of your countries. Which
    variety in which country had the lowest mean weight?
8.  Using your filtered data set from question 6, plot pumpkin weight
    distributions (in either lbs or kg) for your three countries as a
    boxplot. Ensure the plot has appropriate axis labels and is clear
    and well presented. Save this boxplot to your computer.
9.  Redraw your plot from question 8 as a facet plot showing the data
    from each variety of pumpkin as a separate sub-plot. Save this plot
    to your computer.

#### Your github repository should include:

1.  A single R or Python script named `script.R` or `script.py`,
    containing the code you used to answer the questions above.
2.  A text file named `requirements.txt` containing a list of the R
    packages or python modules that need to be installed for your code
    to run.
3.  A document named `output` containing the answers to questions above
    and the three plots you generated in questions 5,8 and 9. Include a
    few sentences summarising what each of the plots shows. This
    document can be in a format of your choosing so the file extension
    will depend on the document type you choose.
4.  A csv file containing the filtered data set that you saved to your
    computer in question 6 named `pumpkins_filtered.csv`
5.  Your completed R or Python notebook (whichever language you used to
    complete the pumpkins task).

You can create a zip download of your github repository once you have
completed all parts of the coursework and uploaded all your files by
clicking the green ‘code’ button at the top right-hand side of your
repository and then selecting ‘Download ZIP’.

Please upload this zip file to the Moodle Coursework submission box on
the LIFE4138 page.

## The differential gene expression analysis challenge

### Your task

For this part of the coursework, you are tasked with writing a script in
either Python or R to process the output of a DESeq2 differential
expression analysis (DGEA). The input will be a TSV file containing the
results from different experimental conditions. Your goal is to output a
detailed report that includes a variety of statistical analyses,
visualisations, and summaries of the results.

To find your data, look in the datasets folder and take the set
corresponding to your name.

### The data

Input Data: TSV files containing the results of DESeq2 differential
expression analysis for different conditions. Each file includes gene
identifiers, log fold changes, p-values, and adjusted p-values.

Please note: you are not expected to run DeSeq2 for yourselves.

### Report Generation:

The output of your script should be a comprehensive report that includes
the following elements:

#### Summary Statistics:

Number of significantly upregulated and downregulated genes (based on
p-value and fold change thresholds) for each comparison. Summary of
p-values and log fold changes across all genes for each comparison.

#### Plots:

Volcano plots to visualize the significance and magnitude of changes in
gene expression for each comparison.

MA plot to display the relationship between the log fold change and mean
expression.

Histogram of p-values to assess the distribution of statistical
significance.

Heatmap of the top differentially expressed genes to illustrate gene
expression patterns across the conditions.

#### Significant Gene Lists:

A table or list of significantly upregulated and downregulated genes
with their corresponding fold changes, p-values, and adjusted p-values.

#### Additional Analyses:

Any relevant insights, such as potential biological pathways affected by
differentially expressed genes or clustering of gene expression
patterns.

You should consider any checks for data quality before generating plots.

### Requirements:

Your script should be able to handle the input data, process it, and
output the results in a clear, organized format. You may choose either
Python or R for the analysis, but the final report should include clear
and interpretable results, regardless of the programming language used.
The script should take as input two tsv files and generate all plots and
tables that you use in your subsequent report.

An ideal report will be well-structured, including headers, legends, and
captions for each plot to ensure readability and clarity of the results.

Your code needs to run on unseen tsv files. It should also include error
handling for missing values or malformed input data.

### Your github repository should include:

1.  A single R or Python script named `script.R` or `script.py`,
    containing the code you used to answer the questions above.
2.  A text file named `requirements.txt` containing a list of the R
    packages or python modules that need to be installed for your code
    to run.
3.  A document named `output` containing the plots and tables generated
    by your code. You may add additional commentary and explanation to
    these plots. This document can be in a format of your choosing so
    the file extension will depend on the document type you choose.

You can create a zip download of your github repository once you have
completed the coursework and uploaded all your files by clicking the
green ‘code’ button at the top right-hand side of your repository and
then selecting ‘Download ZIP’.

Please upload this zip file to the Moodle Coursework submission box on
the LIFE4138 page.
